title: Theory, Limits and Practice
intro: What a quantum reservoir can and cannot compute, what it costs as it grows, where a quantum advantage could come from, and a complete reservoir you can run in numpy.

blocks.text: Every quantum reservoir on this shelf, whatever its hardware, is the same mathematical object: an input-driven quantum channel followed by a linear readout. The state is updated once per input, the features are expectation values, and only the readout weights are trained:

blocks.caption: The input-driven channel $\mathcal{T}_s$ (CPTP for each input $s$), the measured observables $O_i$, and the trained readout $(w, b)$.

blocks.text: Theory asks four questions of this object, and this topic takes them in turn. Which input-output maps can $\hat y_k$ approximate at all (expressivity)? How much of the exponentially large state space survives measurement at finite shots (concentration and scalability)? When does any of it beat a classical model of the same cost (advantage)? And, concretely, how does one build and test one (practice)?

items: Fading memory plus a point-separating family closed under products gives universality: with the echo state property and product reservoirs (tensor products, whose readouts multiply), the outputs are dense in the fading-memory filters, by the Stone–Weierstrass argument Boyd and Chua used for Volterra series. See Expressivity and Universality (#/qrc/theory/expressivity-and-universality).

Features are linear in $\rho_k$, so the readout can never use more than $4^n - 1$ independent directions per time step, and the total information-processing capacity is bounded by the number of linearly independent features.

The input enters only through how $\mathcal{T}_s$ depends on $s$. With reset encoding, $\mathcal{T}_s = \mathcal{T}_0 + s\,\mathcal{T}_1 + \sqrt{s(1-s)}\,\mathcal{T}_2$, so every output is a sum of products over past steps of functions in $\mathrm{span}\{1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)}\}$: rich in cross-time products, poor in single-input nonlinearity.

If the dynamics scramble like a random unitary, a Pauli expectation's spread over inputs falls as $1/\sqrt{2^n+1}$, so the shots needed to read it grow as $2^n$. Large Hilbert space is not large usable feature space. See Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability).

Expressivity and Universality (#/qrc/theory/expressivity-and-universality): fading-memory filters, the Stone–Weierstrass route to universality, the polynomial structure that encoding imposes, feature-rank and capacity bounds.

Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability): exponential concentration from scrambling and from noise, the shot cost of reading features, the restart cost of measurement, and what classical simulation costs.
Quantum Advantage (#/qrc/theory/quantum-advantage): what would count as an advantage, the arguments for and against, classically simulable reservoirs, and how to run a fair comparison.
Hands-on Implementation (#/qrc/theory/hands-on-implementation): a complete numpy quantum reservoir, from Hamiltonian to memory capacity and NARMA2, with every output shown as run.
Open Problems (#/qrc/theory/open-problems): what is not known yet, with pointers into the literature, and a set of self-test questions across the shelf.

blocks.text: Read this topic after The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir) and Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points): the arguments here use the reset-injection model from the first and the contraction ideas from the second.
